sets.description: Work through the original 20 formulas. Choose both the compound name and ionic or covalent type. Each answer is checked separately; use Type answers whenever you want to practice recall.

rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Ba is barium, a group-2 metal. Recognize CO₃ as carbonate, a whole polyatomic ion. Look up that group rather than treating its C and O as separate pieces. | 2. Decide the type: Ba²⁺ and CO₃²⁻ are oppositely charged ions, so classify the compound as ionic. The C–O bonds inside carbonate are covalent, but the compound is held together between positive and negative ions. | 3. Build the answer: Barium is Ba2+ and carbonate is the whole CO3 2− ion. Their charges balance in a 1:1 ratio. Keep carbonate intact; the compound is ionic even though carbonate contains covalent bonds. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Carbonate is not carbide: carbide has no oxygen. Carbonite is not the carbonate name in this course. Barium has the usual +2 charge, so barium(III) does not fit.

namingBoundary.boundary: Between positive and negative ions: ionic naming. Inside each polyatomic ion: covalent bonding. Both descriptions can be true because they describe different parts of the substance.

namingBoundary.constituents: 1 x Ba (charge +2) and 1 x CO3 (charge -2). Total: +2 + (-2) = 0.
namingBoundary.grammar: Name the cation, then the anion: barium carbonate. Keep polyatomic names intact; use a Roman numeral for a variable-charge metal. No molecular counting prefixes.
namingBoundary.name: barium carbonate

rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: K is potassium, a group-1 metal; Cl is chlorine, a nonmetal. In this salt the pieces are K⁺ and Cl⁻, not neutral KCl molecules. | 2. Decide the type: The oppositely charged ions make this ionic. Group 1 helps you find potassium’s +1 charge; chloride supplies −1. | 3. Build the answer: Potassium forms K+ and chloride is Cl−. A 1:1 ratio balances charge. Name the metal first, then chloride; no molecular prefix or Roman numeral is needed for this fixed-charge metal. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Chloride has no oxygen; chlorate is ClO₃⁻. The 1:1 ratio needs neither di- nor a Roman numeral for potassium.

namingBoundary.boundary: Between positive and negative ions: ionic naming. The whole compound is charge balanced; individual ions still have their own charges.
namingBoundary.caution: Use the smallest whole-ion ratio; do not change the formula inside an ion. This is introductory naming bookkeeping, not a complete model of electronic structure.
namingBoundary.constituents: 1 x K (charge +1) and 1 x Cl (charge -1). Total: +1 + (-1) = 0.
namingBoundary.grammar: Name the cation, then the anion: potassium chloride. Keep polyatomic names intact; use a Roman numeral for a variable-charge metal. No molecular counting prefixes.
namingBoundary.name: potassium chloride

rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Pb is the metal lead and Cl is the nonmetal chlorine. In this example, treat each chlorine as a chloride ion, Cl⁻. Lead can have more than one charge. | 2. Decide the type: This is ionic: lead cations balance chloride anions. The formula contains two Cl⁻ ions, so one Pb ion must be +2 for a neutral total. | 3. Build the answer: Two chloride ions contribute −2 in total, so the one lead ion is +2. The Roman numeral II specifies that charge, not the number of chloride ions. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Lead(IV) would require four Cl⁻ ions per lead. Lead(I) would require one. Roman numerals identify the metal charge; do not use the molecular prefix di- to name this salt.

namingBoundary.boundary: Between positive and negative ions: ionic naming. The whole compound is charge balanced; individual ions still have their own charges.
namingBoundary.caution: Use the smallest whole-ion ratio; do not change the formula inside an ion. This is introductory naming bookkeeping, not a complete model of electronic structure.
namingBoundary.constituents: 1 x Pb (charge +2) and 2 x Cl (charge -1). Total: +2 + (-2) = 0.
namingBoundary.grammar: Name the cation, then the anion: lead(II) chloride. Keep polyatomic names intact; use a Roman numeral for a variable-charge metal. No molecular counting prefixes.
namingBoundary.name: lead(II) chloride

rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: S is sulfur and F is fluorine: both are nonmetals. SF₄ is one of this worksheet’s molecular examples; do not try to assign S⁴⁺ and four F⁻ ions just from its subscripts. | 2. Decide the type: Classify SF₄ as covalent. Its atoms are bonded by shared electron pairs, and the formula tells us one sulfur atom and four fluorine atoms. | 3. Build the answer: This is a molecular covalent compound. Four fluorine atoms give tetrafluoride; the first element is sulfur, with no mono- prefix for one atom. Prefixes count atoms rather than ionic charges. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Tetra- means four, so difluoride would give only two F atoms. Tetrasulfur would put four atoms on the wrong element. The missing prefix on sulfur means one, not zero.

rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Fe is the metal iron; S is sulfur. Here sulfur is the monatomic sulfide ion, S²⁻. This is not the oxygen-containing sulfate group, SO₄²⁻. | 2. Decide the type: Iron and sulfide are the cation and anion, so this example is ionic. One Fe must supply +2 to balance one S²⁻. | 3. Build the answer: Sulfide is S2−. A single iron ion must supply +2, so the name is iron(II) sulfide. Sulfide and sulfate are different ions; sulfate contains oxygen. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Iron(III) would not balance this 1:1 sulfide formula. Sulfate would require oxygen, which FeS does not contain. The ending -ide tells you which anion is meant, but does not by itself prove ionic bonding.

rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: N is nitrogen and S is sulfur; both are nonmetals. Read N₂S₃ as the supplied binary covalent formula, with two N atoms and three S atoms. | 2. Decide the type: Use the covalent naming route: count the atoms named by prefixes. There is no metal cation whose charge needs a Roman numeral here. | 3. Build the answer: For this binary covalent formula, di- counts two nitrogen atoms and tri- counts three sulfur atoms. Change the second element ending to -ide: trisulfide. Do not reduce the atom counts. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Tri- belongs to sulfur and di- belongs to nitrogen. Trinitrogen disulfide reverses those counts. Sulfate contains oxygen, which this formula has none of.

Decide the type: Ca²⁺ balances two OH⁻ ions, making this ionic. Covalent bonds inside OH⁻ do not change the classification of the whole calcium hydroxide compound. | 3. Build the answer: Calcium is Ca2+ and each hydroxide group is OH−. Two intact hydroxide ions balance one calcium ion. The parentheses multiply the whole OH group; ionic naming does not use dihydroxide here. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Oxide is O²⁻ and lacks hydrogen. The 2 outside the parentheses multiplies the entire OH group. It does not mean the ionic name must contain dihydroxide.

rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Co is cobalt, a metal, while F is fluorine. Notice the lowercase o: Co is one element; CO would be carbon and oxygen. | 2. Decide the type: This compound is ionic in the course model. Three F⁻ ions contribute −3, so the single cobalt ion must be Co³⁺. | 3. Build the answer: Three fluoride ions contribute −3, so cobalt must be +3. Use cobalt(III) fluoride for this ionic compound. Co is cobalt; CO would mean carbon and oxygen. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: The Roman numeral must be III. Cobalt(II) would pair with two fluorides instead. Trifluoride counts atoms, but this worksheet uses a Roman numeral to specify a variable-charge metal in an ionic salt.

rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Ag is silver, a metal; Br is bromine, a nonmetal. Use the usual course ions Ag⁺ and Br⁻. | 2. Decide the type: Opposite silver and bromide ions balance 1:1, so the compound is ionic. You do not need to see written + and − signs in a neutral salt formula for ions to be present. | 3. Build the answer: The usual course ion for silver is Ag+; bromide is Br−. Their 1:1 combination is silver bromide. Bromate would contain oxygen and is a different ion. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Bromate is BrO₃⁻, so it would add oxygen. Silver(II) and dibromide do not fit the usual +1 silver ion and the printed 1:1 formula.

rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: K is a group-1 metal. SO₄ is the sulfate group: one S and four O atoms belong to each SO₄²⁻ ion. | 2. Decide the type: Two K⁺ ions balance one SO₄²⁻ ion, so classify the whole compound as ionic. More than two different elements does not make a compound covalent. | 3. Build the answer: Sulfate is SO4 2−. Two K+ ions balance one sulfate ion. Retain the polyatomic name sulfate and do not add a molecular prefix to potassium. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Sulfite is SO₃²⁻; sulfide is S²⁻. Neither preserves the four oxygens of sulfate. The ionic name does not use dipotassium just because two potassium ions are needed.

rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Na is sodium, a group-1 metal. OH is the hydroxide group, OH⁻; it is not an oxide plus a separate hydrogen atom in this naming task. | 2. Decide the type: Na⁺ and OH⁻ balance 1:1. The compound is ionic even though the bond within the hydroxide ion is covalent. | 3. Build the answer: Na+ balances one OH− ion. OH− is hydroxide, so the ionic compound is sodium hydroxide. The hydrogen belongs to that whole polyatomic ion. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Sodium oxide would use O²⁻ without hydrogen. Hydroxide is a name worth recognizing as a whole unit. Sodium’s usual +1 charge does not call for sodium(II).

Three oxide ions total −6; two iron ions must total +6, so each is Fe³⁺. | 3. Build the answer: Three oxide ions contribute −6. Two iron ions share +6, making each Fe3+. The Roman numeral is III, not II from the iron subscript. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Use III for the charge on each iron. The subscript 2 counts iron ions and does not mean iron(II). Diiron trioxide follows atom-count naming, while this task uses the ionic Stock name.

Decide the type: Manganese cations and sulfate anions make this ionic. One sulfate contributes −2, so one manganese must be +2 here. | 3. Build the answer: One sulfate ion has charge −2, so Mn must be +2 here: manganese(II) sulfate. Mn is manganese; Mg is magnesium. The sulfate subscript 4 counts oxygen atoms and is not the metal charge. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: The 4 counts oxygen atoms inside sulfate; it does not make manganese(IV). Sulfite has only three oxygens, and magnesium is a different element.

Two chlorides contribute −2, so one iron must be Fe²⁺. | 3. Build the answer: Two Cl− ions balance Fe2+. The name iron(II) chloride specifies the iron charge. Molecular prefixes such as di- are not used for this ionic salt. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Iron(III) would need three chloride ions. The name’s Roman numeral gives iron’s charge. rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: This is the important no-metal case: recognize NH₄⁺ as ammonium and NO₃⁻ as nitrate. They are two whole polyatomic ions, even though every element present is a nonmetal. | 2. Decide the type: Ammonium is positive and nitrate is negative. Attraction between those ions makes the compound ionic. Bonds within each ion are covalent; the question asks about the compound as a whole. | 3. Build the answer: NH4+ is ammonium and NO3− is nitrate. These oppositely charged polyatomic ions form an ionic compound even though no metal appears. Bonds within each ion are covalent; the requested type describes the compound. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Do not choose covalent only because no metal appears. Ammonia is neutral NH₃, not NH₄⁺. Nitrite is NO₂⁻, not the nitrate group printed here.

namingBoundary.boundary: Between positive and negative ions: ionic naming. Inside each polyatomic ion: covalent bonding. Both descriptions can be true because they describe different parts of the substance.
namingBoundary.caution: Ammonium is a positive ion even though it contains no metal. No metal does not necessarily mean molecular.
namingBoundary.constituents: 1 x NH4 (charge +1) and 1 x NO3 (charge -1). Total: +1 + (-1) = 0.

rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Mg is magnesium, a group-2 metal; O is oxygen. The usual ions for this example are Mg²⁺ and oxide, O²⁻. | 2. Decide the type: Oppositely charged ions make this ionic. Equal +2 and −2 charges balance in a 1:1 ratio; no written subscript is needed for one of each. | 3. Build the answer: Mg2+ and O2− balance in the smallest 1:1 ratio. The ionic name is magnesium oxide. Peroxide is O2 2−, a different ion; mono- is not needed here. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Oxide and peroxide are different ions: peroxide is O₂²⁻. Molecular prefixes such as mono- are not needed to name this ionic compound.

namingBoundary.boundary: Between positive and negative ions: ionic naming. The whole compound is charge balanced; individual ions still have their own charges.

namingBoundary.constituents: 1 x Mg (charge +2) and 1 x O (charge -2). Total: +2 + (-2) = 0.

rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: P and O are both nonmetals. For this worksheet, follow the covalent naming route for the printed P₂O₅ formula. | 2. Decide the type: Covalent naming uses the atom counts shown: two phosphorus atoms and five oxygen atoms. Do not invent a monatomic P⁵⁺ ion from an oxidation-state calculation. | 3. Build the answer: Name the formula as printed: di- for two phosphorus atoms and pentoxide for five oxygens. Pentaoxide is also accepted. P2O5 is the conventional empirical representation of phosphorus(V) oxide; common molecular forms use P4O10. This task names the supplied formula and does not silently replace it. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Di- belongs to phosphorus and pent-oxide to oxygen. This printed P₂O₅ is the conventional empirical representation; common molecular forms use P₄O₁₀. Name what is printed here rather than silently replacing the formula.

namingBoundary.boundary: Covalent naming for this reviewed representation. Do not invent ion charges from subscripts or classify every nonmetal solid as molecular.
namingBoundary.caution: This course names the printed empirical representation. Consult the course convention before equating it with a molecular formula.

rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Cu is copper, a variable-charge metal. S is sulfide, S²⁻, in this salt. | 2. Decide the type: This is ionic. One sulfide contributes −2; the two copper ions together must contribute +2, making each Cu⁺. | 3. Build the answer: Sulfide contributes −2. Two copper ions must each contribute +1, so the correct Roman numeral is I. The subscript 2 is the copper count, not its charge. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: The Roman numeral is I. The subscript 2 counts copper ions, not their charge. Copper(II) sulfide would use CuS, and sulfate would require oxygen.

rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: B is boron, a metalloid; Cl is chlorine, a nonmetal. BCl₃ is a known molecular covalent example. Being left of chlorine on the periodic table is not enough to call boron a metal cation. | 2. Decide the type: Use the covalent route: one B atom and three Cl atoms are joined by shared-electron bonds. Boron halides are a useful boundary of the simple metal/nonmetal shortcut. | 3. Build the answer: Boron trichloride is a molecular covalent compound: one boron and three chlorine atoms. Boron is a metalloid, so a metal/nonmetal shortcut alone is not enough; use this known molecular example and its prefixes. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Tri- means three chlorines. Dichloride would mean two, and triboron would put three atoms on the wrong element. Do not infer ionic bonding merely because a formula is neutral.

Decide the type: Three Zn²⁺ ions total +6, and two phosphate ions total −6. These cations and anions make the compound ionic; parentheses preserve repeated polyatomic groups. | 3. Build the answer: Three Zn2+ ions give +6 and two PO4 3− ions give −6. Name the whole phosphate ion. Zinc uses the usual +2 course charge, so the subscript 3 is not a Roman numeral III. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: The subscript 3 counts zinc ions, not a zinc(III) charge. Phosphide is P³⁻ without oxygen; phosphite has a different oxygen count from phosphate.

sets.description: Translate each of the original 10 names into a formula. Ionic compounds use balanced whole-ion ratios; molecular prefixes specify atom counts. Choose answers first, or switch to typing.

Decide the type: Use the ionic route. One +2 nickel ion balances one −2 sulfide ion, so the smallest whole-ion ratio is 1:1. | 3. Build the answer: Nickel(II) is Ni2+ and sulfide is S2−. The smallest neutral ratio is 1:1: NiS. Roman numeral II sets the ion charge; it does not become a subscript automatically. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Do not copy the Roman numeral into Ni₂S: that would leave net +2. NiS₂ would leave net −2. Sulfide contains no oxygen, unlike sulfate.

Decide the type: This is ionic: one positive lithium ion balances one negative hydroxide ion. Keep O and H together while balancing. | 3. Build the answer: Li+ and OH− combine 1:1. Keep hydroxide as OH; with only one hydroxide group, LiOH needs no parentheses. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Li₂OH would total +1; Li(OH)₂ would total −1. LiO leaves out hydrogen and substitutes oxide for hydroxide. One OH group needs no parentheses.

Decide the type: Use the covalent route. No prefix on nitrogen means one N atom; tribromide means three Br atoms. Do not cross ion charges to find these numbers. | 3. Build the answer: The first element has one atom when no prefix is written; tri- means three bromine atoms. The molecular formula is NBr3. Element-symbol capitals matter. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: N₃Br reverses which element gets three atoms. NBr loses the tri- information. N₂Br₃ invents a di- prefix that the name does not contain.

namingBoundary.boundary: Covalent naming for this reviewed representation. Do not invent ion charges from subscripts or classify every nonmetal solid as molecular.

Decide the type: Use the ionic route. Two +1 ammonium ions balance one −2 sulfide ion. The whole ammonium group must be copied twice. | 3. Build the answer: Ammonium is NH4+ and sulfide is S2−. Use two intact ammonium ions for one sulfide ion: (NH4)2S. Parentheses multiply all four hydrogens as well as nitrogen. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: NH₄S supplies only +1 against −2. The 2 belongs outside (NH₄), so it multiplies both N and all four H atoms. N₂H₄S fails to copy the complete ion twice.

One magnesium ion and one sulfide ion cancel to zero, so use the simplest 1:1 whole-ion ratio. | 3. Build the answer: Mg2+ balances S2− in a 1:1 ratio: MgS. Reduce the whole-ion ratio rather than writing Mg2S2. Sulfide contains no oxygen. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Do not keep 2 and 2 as subscripts after crossing charges: Mg₂S₂ reduces to MgS for this ionic formula. Sulfate would include oxygen and answer a different question.

rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Potassium is K⁺, a group-1 metal ion. Sulfate is SO₄²⁻; its four oxygens are part of each ion. | 2. Decide the type: Use the ionic route. Two potassium ions give +2, balancing one sulfate ion with −2. Change only the number of whole ions. | 3. Build the answer: Two K+ ions balance SO4 2−. The formula is K2SO4. Do not change the internal SO4 formula while balancing the ions. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: KSO₄ would still total −1. K₂SO₃ changes sulfate into sulfite. Do not change an ion’s internal subscripts while trying to balance charge.

rows.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Nitrogen and oxygen are nonmetals. Di- and tetr(a)- are atom-count clues in this molecular name. | 2. Decide the type: Use the covalent route. Dinitrogen gives two N atoms and tetroxide gives four O atoms. These are actual molecular counts, not charges to balance. | 3. Build the answer: Di- means two nitrogen atoms and tetr(a)-oxide means four oxygens: N2O4. This is a molecular formula; reducing it to the empirical ratio NO2 names a different molecular species. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: N₂O₄ must not be reduced to NO₂: that would describe a different molecular species. Ionic formulas use smallest whole-ion ratios; molecular formulas preserve the stated atom counts.

Two chlorate ions, each −1, balance one Mg²⁺. Copy the whole ClO₃ group twice. | 3. Build the answer: Mg2+ needs two chlorate ions, each ClO3−. Write Mg(ClO3)2 to retain both complete groups. Chlorite is ClO2− and must not be substituted. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: MgClO₃ has only one negative charge. ClO₂⁻ is chlorite, not chlorate. MgClO₆ has one chlorine instead of two and does not preserve two intact chlorate ions.

One +1 silver ion balances one −1 cyanide ion, producing a 1:1 whole-ion ratio. | 3. Build the answer: Ag+ and cyanide, CN−, balance 1:1: AgCN. Keep carbon and nitrogen together; cyanate would include oxygen and is a different ion. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Ag₂CN has net +1 and Ag(CN)₂ has net −1. examCard.body:
# The small map to carry into practice

## Exam-sheet candidate — verify permitted scope before use

This is a study reference candidate, not a claim about current exam permission or completeness. The instructor’s current rules control what may be used during an assessment.

### Translation compass

```text
NAME → known ions + charges → minimum neutral ratio → formula
FORMULA → recognize ions → infer variable charge → cation name + anion name

Neutral ionic-formula ledger:  n_c q_c + n_a q_a = 0
Roman numeral: charge per metal ion in these simple salts, NOT atom count.
Subscript: atom/group count, NOT charge.
Repeat a polyatomic ion: use parentheses.
Reduce whole-ion counts; never dismantle an ion’s internal formula.
```

### Pattern or memory?

| Reconstruct | Retrieve as an anchor |
|---|---|
| count ratio from known charges | name + formula + charge of each polyatomic ion |
| metal charge from a known anion and formula ratio | allowed variable-metal states when name/context is absent |
| nitrate → nitrite within the known family | nitrate is NO₃⁻ in the first place |
| selected group-1/group-2 monatomic charges | exceptions and source-specific entries |

### Useful anchors

| Name | Ion | Nearby contrast |
|---|---|---|
| nitrate | NO₃⁻ | nitrite NO₂⁻ |
| sulfate | SO₄²⁻ | sulfite SO₃²⁻ |
| phosphate | PO₄³⁻ | phosphide P³⁻ is a different kind of ion |
| carbonate | CO₃²⁻ | bicarbonate/hydrogen carbonate HCO₃⁻ |
| hydroxide | OH⁻ | -ide does not guarantee monatomic |
| ammonium | NH₄⁺ | ammonia NH₃ is neutral |
| acetate | C₂H₃O₂⁻ | learn the charge with the name |
| oxide | O²⁻ | peroxide O₂²⁻ |
| chromate | CrO₄²⁻ | dichromate Cr₂O₇²⁻ |
| permanganate | MnO₄⁻ | not a chlorine-ladder operation |

Chlorine staircase: **ClO⁻ hypochlorite → ClO₂⁻ chlorite → ClO₃⁻ chlorate → ClO₄⁻ perchlorate**.

Within a known family, -ate has more O than -ite. The suffix alone does not specify charge or a universal O count. -ine is not an ion suffix rule. Common monatomic negative ions use -ide; hydroxide, cyanide, and peroxide show why the reverse inference fails.

### Two checks worth carrying

```text
Fe₂O₃: 3(−2)=−6; 2 irons share +6 → +3 each → iron(III) oxide.
Al₂(SO₄)₃: 2(+3)+3(−2)=0; sulfate stays SO₄²⁻.
```

Sodium peroxide is **Na₂O₂**, not NaO. Magnesium oxide is **MgO**, not Mg₂O₂. Compare ion counts, not just the digits on the page.

## Ten-minute paper session

First minute: write three anchors from memory, then compare with the reference. Next three minutes: one name→formula and one formula→name example, with charge ledgers. Next three: contrast nitrate/nitrite and oxide/peroxide. Last three: repair one incorrect formula and explain what information the name supplied. Stop there; the module does not need to turn every short session into a full exam.

## Speaking rehearsal

Say the name, identify both ions, say their charges, and state the ratio. Example: “Calcium nitrate. Calcium plus two. Nitrate minus one. One calcium, two nitrates. Ca(NO₃)₂.” Then write it without looking.

## Notebook prompts

“What did I derive, and what did I remember?”  
“What remains true if I change the cation?”  
“Which subscript belongs inside the ion?”  
“What extra information would make this ambiguous name solvable?”

## Later review

Choose a few items for tomorrow and later sessions. Default spacing is specified in 10, but no notifications or automations have been scheduled by this document. The learner decides when the study system should prompt her.

Shared comparison notes

## Two derivations of the same ratio

For aluminum sulfate, use either a common multiple (+6 and −6) or `3a = 2b`. Both establish a = 2 and b = 3 as the smallest positive integers. The app must accept either coherent explanation. “Criss-cross” may be offered after the derivation, but always follow it by a ratio-reduction and group-identity check.

## Contrast worth keeping visible

- FeCl₂ versus FeCl₃: same element names, different iron state.
- KClO₂ versus KClO₃: same cation charge and same anion charge, different anion identity/name.
- MgO versus Na₂O₂: least whole-number **ion** ratio is not least whole-number **atom** ratio in every formula.
- Ca(NO₃)₂ versus CaN₂O₆: distinguish atom-equivalent notation from the preferred grouped representation; teach the improvement without denying what is already correct.

**Target:** NaCl ⇄ sodium chloride. Related seed: PR-17.

1. Recognize Na⁺ as sodium and Cl⁻ as chloride.
2. Build charge totals: 1 × (+1) = +1; 1 × (−1) = −1.
3. Confirm the minimum ion-count ratio 1:1. The total is zero.
4. Write NaCl; name the cation first and preserve the anion name.

**Atom inventory:** Na = 1, Cl = 1. This is a second representation check, not a replacement for charge balance.

**Reflection:** Which information came from an ion anchor, and which part did charge balance determine?

lessons.body:
**Lesson ID:** L01  
**Skills:** SK-01, SK-09  
**Planning duration:** 7 minutes  
**Prerequisites:** None; a periodic table and ion card may remain visible.

## Model change

Before: A superscript, a subscript, and a coefficient all feel like numbers attached to symbols.

After: Each number has a different referent: atoms inside a group, charge of a group, or number of groups.


## Situated opening

> **Ms. Luminara:** “One nitrate ion has arrived. The three is its oxygen inventory. The minus sign is its net charge. They have been filling out different forms.”
>
> **the learner:** “So I cannot read the three as three charges.”
>
> **a peer:** “And putting three nitrates on the ledger means three complete copies.”

Show NO₃⁻, then three identical nitrate tiles. Under the tiles show N = 3, O = 9, total charge = −3. The tiles represent complete ions; a negative icon does not belong separately to each oxygen.

## Teaching sequence

1. Label the subscript 3 and superscript −1 with words before colors. Ask what each describes.
2. Add a second nitrate tile. Keep the individual tile formula unchanged; update group count to 2 and total charge to −2.
3. Place Ca²⁺ beside one Cl⁻. Show `+2 + (−1) = +1` immediately as a ledger, not as a failed experiment.
4. Add the second chloride. Show `+2 + 2(−1) = 0`, then CaCl₂.
5. Return to one NO₃⁻ tile. Explain why that ion is permitted to have nonzero charge even though a neutral compound formula is not.

## Representation links

Spoken: “two chloride ions for one calcium ion.” Written: CaCl₂. Algebra: `1(+2)+2(−1)=0`. Tiles: one +2 card and two −1 cards. Tap each representation and highlight the corresponding whole group in the others, without making color the only cue.

## Fading practice

Worked: CaCl₂. Completion: Na⁺ with O²⁻, where one sodium is already on the ledger. Independent: Mg²⁺ with Cl⁻. Do not reveal final subscripts while asking the learner to retrieve them.

## Misconception catch

If the learner says “everything has to add to zero,” show NO₃⁻ alone next to neutral NaNO₃. Ask which object the neutrality condition describes. Repair the scope, not the arithmetic. Use `D-SCOPE-NEUTRALITY`.

## Under the Floorboards

Show `q/e = Z − N_e` only for a monatomic ion. Polyatomic net charge is the charge on the group, not simply a count of visible oxygen atoms. No bond-formation energy claim is needed yet.

## Slow Turn

Prompt: “What stayed fixed when we added another nitrate tile?” Expected idea: its internal formula and charge; only the number of copies changed. Save an optional notebook sentence locally, without grading its prose.

## Optional aside: charge patterns and energy

For selected main-group monatomic ions, group position predicts useful charges: group 1 +1, group 2 +2, Al/Ga +3, halides −1, oxide/sulfide −2, and nitride/phosphide −3. This restricted pattern does not determine every transition-metal charge or any polyatomic ion formula.

Removing an electron from an isolated gaseous atom costs energy. Noble-gas-like occupancy alone does not explain compound formation; lattice interactions and the rest of the process matter. This is the scoped clarification in RULE-08 of the supplied chemistry rules.
lessons.title: The charge ledger: three different numbers

lessons.body:
**Lesson ID:** L02  
**Skills:** SK-02, SK-03, SK-09  
**Planning duration:** 8 minutes  
**Prerequisites:** SK-01 helps; reference cards remain available.

## Model change

Before: The end of a word is expected to reveal everything about an ion.

After: Names are parsed into recognized identities; selected periodic patterns help with charges but do not replace the ion bank.


## Opening contrast

Show “chlorine,” “chloride,” and “chlorate.” Do not initially ask for all three formulas. Ask which part of each word seems informative. Then reveal: element name; monatomic anion Cl⁻; known oxyanion ClO₃⁻.

> **the learner:** “I was hoping the ending would be a complete decoder.”
>
> **Ms. Luminara:** “It is a clue to the family, not the full address.”

## Teaching sequence

1. Cations first: Na⁺ sodium, Ca²⁺ calcium, Al³⁺ aluminum. Then the nonmetal exception to the metal cue: NH₄⁺ ammonium.
2. Common monatomic anions: Cl⁻ chloride, O²⁻ oxide, N³⁻ nitride. Store names as dictionary entries, not string surgery.
3. Show hydroxide OH⁻ and cyanide CN⁻. Both end in -ide; both contain two elements. Ask what failed in “-ide always means one atom.”
4. Preview only two polyatomic anchors needed next: nitrate NO₃⁻ and sulfate SO₄²⁻. Keep them visible through L03.
5. Contrast fixed-course charges with variable-metal entries Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺. A blank “iron” card cannot choose its charge without context.

## Periodic mini-map

Use clickable group labels, not a complete periodic-table app rebuild. Group 1’s selected entries show +1; group 2 +2. Show Al/Ga specifically rather than asserting every group-13 ion is always +3. Halides −1, oxide/sulfide −2, nitride/phosphide −3 are a scoped introductory set. Transition-metal area displays “use supplied charge or infer from the compound.”

## Memory actions

See Cl⁻, say chloride, cover it, write it back. Repeat later in reverse. Offer the spoken cue “single-atom negative: recognized root plus -ide,” immediately followed by the caveat that the converse is false. Do not let the mnemonic erase hydroxide or peroxide.

## Fading and transfer

Worked: sodium sulfide is made from Na⁺ and S²⁻. Completion: supply the ion cards for magnesium oxide. Independent: identify the two cards in ammonium chloride. The objective here is identity selection, not yet independent ratio derivation.

## Slow Turn

Create two notebook columns, “derived from a pattern” and “retrieved from an anchor.” Place calcium’s +2 in the first, nitrate’s NO₃⁻ identity in the second. Ask: “Which uncertainty do you actually have right now?”
lessons.title: Name badges: what you can predict and what you must recall

lessons.body:
**Lesson ID:** L03  
**Skills:** SK-05, SK-06, SK-10  
**Planning duration:** 10 minutes  
**Prerequisites:** Identify or look up the ion cards. Ion recall is not a prerequisite for practicing charge balance.

## Model change

Before: Crossing numbers feels like a magic rule, and every subscript looks reducible.

After: Counts are the smallest whole-number solution; polyatomic internal subscripts stay part of ion identity.


## Core example

Give Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻. Start at one of each. The ledger reads +1. Allow any attempted counts; show what they imply without rejecting the physical manipulation.

> **a peer:** “Two aluminums make +6. Three sulfate cards make −6. I will try that.”
>
> **Ms. Luminara:** “The ledger balances. Now let the notation report exactly what you built.”

Reveal Al₂(SO₄)₃ only after counts are confirmed. Preserve the sulfate card as a whole while adding an outer multiplier.

## The derivation the learner can inspect

`3a − 2b = 0`. The smallest positive integers are a = 2 and b = 3. A table of trial totals, least common multiple, algebra, or a justified crossing shortcut are all valid ways to get there. Do not grade the presentation of multiplication as if it were the chemistry itself.

## Three contrast pairs

- Mg²⁺ + O²⁻ → MgO. Equal charge magnitudes require one of each.
- Al³⁺ + PO₄³⁻ → AlPO₄. Do not write Al₃(PO₄)₃ as the simplest formula.
- Na⁺ + O₂²⁻ → Na₂O₂. Its two sodium ions and one peroxide ion are already the minimum group ratio. Do not simplify the internal O₂ to O.

## Parentheses lens

For Ca(NO₃)₂ reveal nested counts: one calcium; two nitrate groups; each group contains one N and three O. Show Ca = 1, N = 2, O = 6. Then compare:

- Ca(NO₃)₂: conventional grouped result.
- CaN₂O₆: same atom counts, grouping not expressed as requested.
- CaNO₆: wrong atom counts and no correct nitrate decomposition.
- Ca(NO₃)₃: recognizable groups but the charge ledger is −1.

Use different messages for these different situations.

## Fading practice

Fully work calcium nitrate. Leave the sulfate count blank for aluminum sulfate. Then ask for magnesium phosphate with the ions supplied. A subsequent example changes both charges to +3/−3 to test minimum ratio rather than rote crossing.

## Slow Turn

Ask the learner to complete: “The subscript inside nitrate stayed ___; the subscript outside the parentheses tells me ___.” Expected: three oxygens per nitrate; number of complete nitrate groups. Follow with the peroxide non-reduction test.
lessons.title: Build the formula without changing the passengers

lessons.body:
**Lesson ID:** L04  
**Skills:** SK-07, SK-08  
**Planning duration:** 8 minutes  
**Prerequisites:** SK-01 and known anion charge; the anion card may be shown.

## Model change

Before: The Roman numeral seems to count metal atoms or to be another fact to memorize.

After: For these salts it states charge per metal ion, derived from the total anion charge and number of metal ions.


## The discriminating example

Show Fe₂O₃ beside FeCl₂. Both contain a written 2 somewhere, but their iron charges differ.

For Fe₂O₃: three O²⁻ total −6; two Fe ions must total +6; each Fe is +3; the name is iron(III) oxide. For FeCl₂: two Cl⁻ total −2; one Fe is +2; iron(II) chloride.

> **a peer:** “The three in iron(III) belongs to each iron, not to the number of irons.”
>
> **the learner:** “Then I need to divide the total positive charge by the count of metal ions.”

## Repeatable reverse-translation trace

1. Confirm this is an in-scope ionic-formula exercise.
2. Identify the anion as a whole; retrieve its charge.
3. Read the number of anion units and calculate their total charge.
4. Use neutrality to find the total cation charge.
5. Divide by cation count; compare with allowed charge states.
6. Name the cation, including the numeral where needed, followed by the anion.

Use Cu(NO₃)₂ as the polyatomic follow-up. Do not infer the metal numeral from the oxygen count; infer it from the two nitrate charges.

## Productive ambiguity

“Copper sulfate” lacks the copper state in a name-to-formula item. It is reasonable to ask for clarification. By contrast CuSO₄ provides enough information to infer copper(II). This is a lesson in information available, not a speed test.

Fe₃O₄ yields an average +8/3 if every iron is assumed identical. That is a useful boundary marker: the simple single-charge algorithm is insufficient. Show “mixed-valence extension, outside this lesson,” not iron(VIII/III) oxide or an invented integer.

## Fading

Worked: FeCl₃. Completion: Fe₂O₃ with the total −6 supplied. Independent: Cu₂O. Then transfer to Fe₃(PO₄)₂, where two −3 phosphate groups require three +2 irons.

## Slow Turn

Ask: “When did the formula tell us something the bare metal name did not?” Expected idea: the known partner’s charge and the ratio constrained the metal state. Allow a sentence or a completed charge ledger as the response.
lessons.title: Read backward: let the known ion constrain the unknown

lessons.body:
**Lesson ID:** L05  
**Skills:** SK-02, SK-04, SK-09  
**Planning duration:** 12 minutes  
**Prerequisites:** Basic ion notation. This lesson can be opened before L03 if vocabulary is the main obstacle.

## Model change

Before: -ate, -ite, per-, hypo-, and -ide feel like unrelated syllables or universal atom counters.

After: Families have remembered anchors and local relationships; suffixes do not encode universal oxygen counts or charges.


## Work one family at a time

Start with nitrate NO₃⁻ and nitrite NO₂⁻. Ask what changed and what stayed: one oxygen changes; nitrogen and net −1 remain. The learner may use “ATE ate more oxygen,” but must finish “within this family.”

Next show sulfate SO₄²⁻ and sulfite SO₃²⁻. Compare nitrate and sulfite: both have three oxygens, yet one is -ate and the other -ite. This is the counterexample that prevents the mnemonic becoming a false rule.

## Chlorine staircase

Keep chlorate ClO₃⁻ as the anchor. Reveal the four positions in order:

```text
ClO⁻   hypochlorite
ClO₂⁻  chlorite
ClO₃⁻  chlorate
ClO₄⁻  perchlorate
```

The charge badge stays −1. Moving the interface slider selects a different known ion card; it does not perform a chemical reaction. A “show electrons/oxidation states” extension must explicitly distinguish formal oxidation-state accounting from actual localized charges.

## Other contrast stations

Carbonate CO₃²⁻ versus bicarbonate HCO₃⁻: adding H⁺ to the charge inventory gives −2+1=−1. The H belongs inside the ion; Ca(HCO₃)₂ repeats the whole group.

Oxide O²⁻ versus peroxide O₂²⁻: same net charge; different group identities. Replay the sodium peroxide exception to naive subscript reduction.

Chromate CrO₄²⁻ versus dichromate Cr₂O₇²⁻: recall this pair. Two chromate copies would have different atom totals and total charge. The name is not a command to duplicate the ion card.

Ammonium NH₄⁺ and hydronium H₃O⁺: two useful positive groups. Hydroxide OH⁻ and cyanide CN⁻ demonstrate that -ide is not proof of a monatomic ion.

## Memory micro-cycle

Look → say the name → cover the card → write formula AND charge → reverse the cue later. A drawing or spoken response may replace typing, but a handwritten interpretation requires confirmation before automated feedback. Do not recite the complete 62-ion bank in a single presentation.

## Slow Turn

> **Ástríðr:** “So a pattern can reduce the remembering, but only after we know what family it belongs to.”
>
> **Ms. Luminara:** “Exactly. We keep the anchor and the rule. Throwing away either one sends the bus to the wrong address.”

Have the learner sort statements into “calculate,” “family pattern,” and “remember.” Sulfate’s −2 charge belongs under remember; the number of sulfate groups with Al³⁺ belongs under calculate.
lessons.title: The oxygen family wall: a few anchors, carefully bounded rules

lessons.body:
**Lesson ID:** L06  
**Skills:** SK-08, SK-09, SK-10  
**Planning duration:** 9 plus 3-minute exit minutes  
**Prerequisites:** Any earlier lesson; use the reference if desired.

## Model change

Before: Success on a familiar example may depend on recognizing the displayed answer.

After: The learner can construct and inspect a translation on a new example, identify missing information, and know which anchor needs review.


## The transfer round

Choose six items: two name→formula, two formula→name, one identity contrast, and one scope/ambiguity item. Avoid simply reversing the item shown a moment ago and counting it as fresh evidence. Change the cation or family while preserving the target skill.

Suggested round: PR-23, PR-34, PR-45, PR-50, PR-62, PR-66. The bank defines prompts; the key defines approved interpretations.

## What the learner does

For each item, permit a final answer immediately. Offer optional expandable steps: identify ions → show charges → choose counts → write conventional form → name. Do not force an expert through every intermediate box. When an answer is wrong, expose the earliest supported mismatch rather than requiring the learner to restart a correct section.

After a correct but uncertain response, show a brief contrasting example and ask what is different. After a high-confidence error, show the charge or atom inventory as evidence, not a chastising message.

## Narrative integration without a penalty mechanism

> **Carlos:** “Can I call Fe₂O₃ iron(II) oxide? There are two irons.”
>
> **the learner:** “That counts the passengers. The numeral labels each passenger’s charge. Three oxides need +6 in total.”
>
> **a peer:** “Two irons sharing +6: +3 each. The ledger settles it.”
>
> **Ms. Luminara:** “There is the translation. No one needed to appeal to the driver’s authority.”

The story demonstration is unscored. Independent retrieval is a separate chosen mode. No student or learner is punished, trapped, or humiliated for a wrong answer.

## Exit artifact

Create a private three-line field note:

- A rule I can rebuild: ______.
- An identity I still need to retrieve: ______.
- A distinction that helped: ______.

Offer a review queue based on actual attempts, not guessed learner traits. Export the field note only with explicit selection; the public lesson does not contain the learner’s private responses.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Ba is barium, a group-2 metal. Recognize CO₃ as carbonate, a whole polyatomic ion. Look up that group rather than treating its C and O as separate pieces. | 2. Decide the type: Ba²⁺ and CO₃²⁻ are oppositely charged ions, so classify the compound as ionic. The C–O bonds inside carbonate are covalent, but the compound is held together between positive and negative ions. | 3. Build the answer: Barium is Ba2+ and carbonate is the whole CO3 2− ion. Their charges balance in a 1:1 ratio. Keep carbonate intact; the compound is ionic even though carbonate contains covalent bonds. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Carbonate is not carbide: carbide has no oxygen. Carbonite is not the carbonate name in this course. Barium has the usual +2 charge, so barium(III) does not fit.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: K is potassium, a group-1 metal; Cl is chlorine, a nonmetal. In this salt the pieces are K⁺ and Cl⁻, not neutral KCl molecules. | 2. Decide the type: The oppositely charged ions make this ionic. Group 1 helps you find potassium’s +1 charge; chloride supplies −1. | 3. Build the answer: Potassium forms K+ and chloride is Cl−. A 1:1 ratio balances charge. Name the metal first, then chloride; no molecular prefix or Roman numeral is needed for this fixed-charge metal. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Chloride has no oxygen; chlorate is ClO₃⁻. The 1:1 ratio needs neither di- nor a Roman numeral for potassium.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Pb is the metal lead and Cl is the nonmetal chlorine. In this example, treat each chlorine as a chloride ion, Cl⁻. Lead can have more than one charge. | 2. Decide the type: This is ionic: lead cations balance chloride anions. The formula contains two Cl⁻ ions, so one Pb ion must be +2 for a neutral total. | 3. Build the answer: Two chloride ions contribute −2 in total, so the one lead ion is +2. The Roman numeral II specifies that charge, not the number of chloride ions. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Lead(IV) would require four Cl⁻ ions per lead. Lead(I) would require one. Roman numerals identify the metal charge; do not use the molecular prefix di- to name this salt.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: S is sulfur and F is fluorine: both are nonmetals. SF₄ is one of this worksheet’s molecular examples; do not try to assign S⁴⁺ and four F⁻ ions just from its subscripts. | 2. Decide the type: Classify SF₄ as covalent. Its atoms are bonded by shared electron pairs, and the formula tells us one sulfur atom and four fluorine atoms. | 3. Build the answer: This is a molecular covalent compound. Four fluorine atoms give tetrafluoride; the first element is sulfur, with no mono- prefix for one atom. Prefixes count atoms rather than ionic charges. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Tetra- means four, so difluoride would give only two F atoms. Tetrasulfur would put four atoms on the wrong element. The missing prefix on sulfur means one, not zero.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Fe is the metal iron; S is sulfur. Here sulfur is the monatomic sulfide ion, S²⁻. This is not the oxygen-containing sulfate group, SO₄²⁻. | 2. Decide the type: Iron and sulfide are the cation and anion, so this example is ionic. One Fe must supply +2 to balance one S²⁻. | 3. Build the answer: Sulfide is S2−. A single iron ion must supply +2, so the name is iron(II) sulfide. Sulfide and sulfate are different ions; sulfate contains oxygen. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Iron(III) would not balance this 1:1 sulfide formula. Sulfate would require oxygen, which FeS does not contain. The ending -ide tells you which anion is meant, but does not by itself prove ionic bonding.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: N is nitrogen and S is sulfur; both are nonmetals. Read N₂S₃ as the supplied binary covalent formula, with two N atoms and three S atoms. | 2. Decide the type: Use the covalent naming route: count the atoms named by prefixes. There is no metal cation whose charge needs a Roman numeral here. | 3. Build the answer: For this binary covalent formula, di- counts two nitrogen atoms and tri- counts three sulfur atoms. Change the second element ending to -ide: trisulfide. Do not reduce the atom counts. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Tri- belongs to sulfur and di- belongs to nitrogen. Trinitrogen disulfide reverses those counts. Sulfate contains oxygen, which this formula has none of.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Ca is calcium, a group-2 metal. The parentheses show repeated OH groups; OH⁻ is the hydroxide ion. Keep each O and H together. | 2. Decide the type: Ca²⁺ balances two OH⁻ ions, making this ionic. Covalent bonds inside OH⁻ do not change the classification of the whole calcium hydroxide compound. | 3. Build the answer: Calcium is Ca2+ and each hydroxide group is OH−. Two intact hydroxide ions balance one calcium ion. The parentheses multiply the whole OH group; ionic naming does not use dihydroxide here. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Oxide is O²⁻ and lacks hydrogen. The 2 outside the parentheses multiplies the entire OH group. It does not mean the ionic name must contain dihydroxide.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Co is cobalt, a metal, while F is fluorine. Notice the lowercase o: Co is one element; CO would be carbon and oxygen. | 2. Decide the type: This compound is ionic in the course model. Three F⁻ ions contribute −3, so the single cobalt ion must be Co³⁺. | 3. Build the answer: Three fluoride ions contribute −3, so cobalt must be +3. Use cobalt(III) fluoride for this ionic compound. Co is cobalt; CO would mean carbon and oxygen. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: The Roman numeral must be III. Cobalt(II) would pair with two fluorides instead. Trifluoride counts atoms, but this worksheet uses a Roman numeral to specify a variable-charge metal in an ionic salt.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: K is a group-1 metal. SO₄ is the sulfate group: one S and four O atoms belong to each SO₄²⁻ ion. | 2. Decide the type: Two K⁺ ions balance one SO₄²⁻ ion, so classify the whole compound as ionic. More than two different elements does not make a compound covalent. | 3. Build the answer: Sulfate is SO4 2−. Two K+ ions balance one sulfate ion. Retain the polyatomic name sulfate and do not add a molecular prefix to potassium. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Sulfite is SO₃²⁻; sulfide is S²⁻. Neither preserves the four oxygens of sulfate. The ionic name does not use dipotassium just because two potassium ions are needed.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Na is sodium, a group-1 metal. OH is the hydroxide group, OH⁻; it is not an oxide plus a separate hydrogen atom in this naming task. | 2. Decide the type: Na⁺ and OH⁻ balance 1:1. The compound is ionic even though the bond within the hydroxide ion is covalent. | 3. Build the answer: Na+ balances one OH− ion. OH− is hydroxide, so the ionic compound is sodium hydroxide. The hydrogen belongs to that whole polyatomic ion. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Sodium oxide would use O²⁻ without hydrogen. Hydroxide is a name worth recognizing as a whole unit. Sodium’s usual +1 charge does not call for sodium(II).

Three oxide ions total −6; two iron ions must total +6, so each is Fe³⁺. | 3. Build the answer: Three oxide ions contribute −6. Two iron ions share +6, making each Fe3+. The Roman numeral is III, not II from the iron subscript. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Use III for the charge on each iron. The subscript 2 counts iron ions and does not mean iron(II). Diiron trioxide follows atom-count naming, while this task uses the ionic Stock name.

Decide the type: Manganese cations and sulfate anions make this ionic. One sulfate contributes −2, so one manganese must be +2 here. | 3. Build the answer: One sulfate ion has charge −2, so Mn must be +2 here: manganese(II) sulfate. Mn is manganese; Mg is magnesium. The sulfate subscript 4 counts oxygen atoms and is not the metal charge. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: The 4 counts oxygen atoms inside sulfate; it does not make manganese(IV). Sulfite has only three oxygens, and magnesium is a different element.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: This is the important no-metal case: recognize NH₄⁺ as ammonium and NO₃⁻ as nitrate. They are two whole polyatomic ions, even though every element present is a nonmetal. | 2. Decide the type: Ammonium is positive and nitrate is negative. Attraction between those ions makes the compound ionic. Bonds within each ion are covalent; the question asks about the compound as a whole. | 3. Build the answer: NH4+ is ammonium and NO3− is nitrate. These oppositely charged polyatomic ions form an ionic compound even though no metal appears. Bonds within each ion are covalent; the requested type describes the compound. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Do not choose covalent only because no metal appears. Ammonia is neutral NH₃, not NH₄⁺. Nitrite is NO₂⁻, not the nitrate group printed here.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Mg is magnesium, a group-2 metal; O is oxygen. The usual ions for this example are Mg²⁺ and oxide, O²⁻. | 2. Decide the type: Oppositely charged ions make this ionic. Equal +2 and −2 charges balance in a 1:1 ratio; no written subscript is needed for one of each. | 3. Build the answer: Mg2+ and O2− balance in the smallest 1:1 ratio. The ionic name is magnesium oxide. Peroxide is O2 2−, a different ion; mono- is not needed here. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Oxide and peroxide are different ions: peroxide is O₂²⁻. Molecular prefixes such as mono- are not needed to name this ionic compound.

Build the answer: Name the formula as printed: di- for two phosphorus atoms and pentoxide for five oxygens. Pentaoxide is also accepted. Name what is printed here rather than silently replacing the formula.

Build the answer: Name the formula as printed: di- for two phosphorus atoms and pentoxide for five oxygens. Pentaoxide is also accepted. P2O5 is the conventional empirical representation of phosphorus(V) oxide; common molecular forms use P4O10. This task names the supplied formula and does not silently replace it. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Di- belongs to phosphorus and pent-oxide to oxygen. This printed P₂O₅ is the conventional empirical representation; common molecular forms use P₄O₁₀. Name what is printed here rather than silently replacing the formula.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Cu is copper, a variable-charge metal. S is sulfide, S²⁻, in this salt. | 2. Decide the type: This is ionic. One sulfide contributes −2; the two copper ions together must contribute +2, making each Cu⁺. | 3. Build the answer: Sulfide contributes −2. Two copper ions must each contribute +1, so the correct Roman numeral is I. The subscript 2 is the copper count, not its charge. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: The Roman numeral is I. The subscript 2 counts copper ions, not their charge. Copper(II) sulfide would use CuS, and sulfate would require oxygen.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: B is boron, a metalloid; Cl is chlorine, a nonmetal. BCl₃ is a known molecular covalent example. Being left of chlorine on the periodic table is not enough to call boron a metal cation. | 2. Decide the type: Use the covalent route: one B atom and three Cl atoms are joined by shared-electron bonds. Boron halides are a useful boundary of the simple metal/nonmetal shortcut. | 3. Build the answer: Boron trichloride is a molecular covalent compound: one boron and three chlorine atoms. Boron is a metalloid, so a metal/nonmetal shortcut alone is not enough; use this known molecular example and its prefixes. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Tri- means three chlorines. Dichloride would mean two, and triboron would put three atoms on the wrong element. Do not infer ionic bonding merely because a formula is neutral.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Zn is zinc, a metal using the usual +2 course charge. PO₄ is phosphate, a whole PO₄³⁻ ion. | 2. Decide the type: Three Zn²⁺ ions total +6, and two phosphate ions total −6. These cations and anions make the compound ionic; parentheses preserve repeated polyatomic groups. | 3. Build the answer: Three Zn2+ ions give +6 and two PO4 3− ions give −6. Name the whole phosphate ion. Zinc uses the usual +2 course charge, so the subscript 3 is not a Roman numeral III. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: The subscript 3 counts zinc ions, not a zinc(III) charge. Phosphide is P³⁻ without oxygen; phosphite has a different oxygen count from phosphate.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Nickel is a metal; the Roman numeral (II) explicitly gives Ni²⁺. Sulfide is S²⁻. Identify those two ions before deciding subscripts. | 2. Decide the type: Use the ionic route. One +2 nickel ion balances one −2 sulfide ion, so the smallest whole-ion ratio is 1:1. | 3. Build the answer: Nickel(II) is Ni2+ and sulfide is S2−. The smallest neutral ratio is 1:1: NiS. Roman numeral II sets the ion charge; it does not become a subscript automatically. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Do not copy the Roman numeral into Ni₂S: that would leave net +2. NiS₂ would leave net −2. Sulfide contains no oxygen, unlike sulfate.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Lithium is a group-1 metal, so use Li⁺. Hydroxide means the whole OH⁻ ion. | 2. Decide the type: This is ionic: one positive lithium ion balances one negative hydroxide ion. Keep O and H together while balancing. | 3. Build the answer: Li+ and OH− combine 1:1. Keep hydroxide as OH; with only one hydroxide group, LiOH needs no parentheses. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Li₂OH would total +1; Li(OH)₂ would total −1. LiO leaves out hydrogen and substitutes oxide for hydroxide. One OH group needs no parentheses.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Nitrogen and bromine are both nonmetals. The name already tells you to use the molecular prefix tri-, which counts atoms. | 2. Decide the type: Use the covalent route. No prefix on nitrogen means one N atom; tribromide means three Br atoms. Do not cross ion charges to find these numbers. | 3. Eliminate alternatives: N₃Br reverses which element gets three atoms. NBr loses the tri- information. N₂Br₃ invents a di- prefix that the name does not contain.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Ammonium is the positive polyatomic ion NH₄⁺, not neutral ammonia NH₃. Sulfide is S²⁻. No metal is needed because ammonium supplies the cation. | 2. Decide the type: Use the ionic route. Two +1 ammonium ions balance one −2 sulfide ion. The whole ammonium group must be copied twice. | 3. Build the answer: Ammonium is NH4+ and sulfide is S2−. Use two intact ammonium ions for one sulfide ion: (NH4)2S. Parentheses multiply all four hydrogens as well as nitrogen. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: NH₄S supplies only +1 against −2. The 2 belongs outside (NH₄), so it multiplies both N and all four H atoms. N₂H₄S fails to copy the complete ion twice.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Magnesium is Mg²⁺, a group-2 metal ion. Sulfide is the monatomic S²⁻ ion. | 2. Decide the type: Use the ionic route. One magnesium ion and one sulfide ion cancel to zero, so use the simplest 1:1 whole-ion ratio. | 3. Build the answer: Mg2+ balances S2− in a 1:1 ratio: MgS. Reduce the whole-ion ratio rather than writing Mg2S2. Sulfide contains no oxygen. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: Do not keep 2 and 2 as subscripts after crossing charges: Mg₂S₂ reduces to MgS for this ionic formula. Sulfate would include oxygen and answer a different question.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Potassium is K⁺, a group-1 metal ion. Sulfate is SO₄²⁻; its four oxygens are part of each ion. | 2. Decide the type: Use the ionic route. Two potassium ions give +2, balancing one sulfate ion with −2. Change only the number of whole ions. | 3. Build the answer: Two K+ ions balance SO4 2−. The formula is K2SO4. Do not change the internal SO4 formula while balancing the ions. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: KSO₄ would still total −1. K₂SO₃ changes sulfate into sulfite. Do not change an ion’s internal subscripts while trying to balance charge.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Nitrogen and oxygen are nonmetals. Di- and tetr(a)- are atom-count clues in this molecular name. | 2. Decide the type: Use the covalent route. Dinitrogen gives two N atoms and tetroxide gives four O atoms. These are actual molecular counts, not charges to balance. | 3. Build the answer: Di- means two nitrogen atoms and tetr(a)-oxide means four oxygens: N2O4. This is a molecular formula; reducing it to the empirical ratio NO2 names a different molecular species. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: N₂O₄ must not be reduced to NO₂: that would describe a different molecular species. Ionic formulas use smallest whole-ion ratios; molecular formulas preserve the stated atom counts.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Magnesium is Mg²⁺. Chlorate is the whole polyatomic ion ClO₃⁻; use the ion list if you do not recognize it yet. | 2. Decide the type: Use the ionic route. Two chlorate ions, each −1, balance one Mg²⁺. Copy the whole ClO₃ group twice. | 3. Build the answer: Mg2+ needs two chlorate ions, each ClO3−. Write Mg(ClO3)2 to retain both complete groups. Chlorite is ClO2− and must not be substituted. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: MgClO₃ has only one negative charge. ClO₂⁻ is chlorite, not chlorate. MgClO₆ has one chlorine instead of two and does not preserve two intact chlorate ions.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: Boron is a metalloid and fluorine a nonmetal. Boron trifluoride is a known molecular covalent compound, not an ordinary metal–anion salt. | 2. Decide the type: Use the covalent route. No prefix on boron means one B atom; tri- on fluoride means three F atoms. Shared electron pairs form the bonds in this molecular example. | 3. Build the answer: Boron trifluoride is a molecular covalent compound. No first prefix means one boron; tri- gives three fluorine atoms. Write BF3 rather than using ionic charge crossing. | 4. Eliminate alternatives: B₃F puts three on boron instead of fluorine. BF and BF₂ lose the tri- count. The octet rule is not a classification test: boron’s incomplete octet here does not make the compound ionic.

practice.explanation: 1. Find the pieces: iron(III) is the positive ion (charge +3); oxide is the negative ion (charge -2). | 2. Decide the type: the compound is ionic because it combines whole positive and negative ions. Any covalent bonds inside a polyatomic ion do not change that classification. | 3. Build the answer: 2 positive group(s) give +6 and 3 negative group(s) give -6; the total is zero. The smallest whole-ion ratio gives Fe2O3, named iron(III) oxide. | 4. Check the scope: III gives the charge on each iron ion, not a subscript to copy. Oxide is O²⁻; balance total positive and negative charge.
hints: Ms. Luminara: first identify the pieces. Is a metal or a named positive ion present, or are you looking at the reviewed molecular naming pattern? Notice a polyatomic ion as one whole group. A subscript counts atoms; it is not automatically a charge.

Use whole positive and negative ions. Name the positive ion first and the negative ion second, retaining a polyatomic ion's name. Balance total charge to zero for the formula.
